passage: Dear Pallavi Di, You asked why I went straight to my room when you visited on Sunday. I want to explain properly. At school I hold my tics in all day. The shrugs, the sniffs, the little squeak. I sit on my hands and count. It's like holding a sneeze for seven hours. By the time I get home I'm so tired I can hardly speak, and then they all come out at once in my room. That's what you heard through the door. Mummy used to say, "Try harder to stop." She doesn't anymore. Last month we saw a doctor who explained what tics are and what options there are if they cause real trouble. Mummy just brings me tea now and closes the door softly. I wasn't upset with you. I was just empty. Love, your cousin-sister Minakshi

qa.q: Where do Minakshi's tics all come out at once?
qa.a: In her room, when she gets home.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel by the time she gets home from school?
qa.a: She feels so tired she can hardly speak, after holding her tics in all day.

qa.q: What change at home helped Minakshi cope better?
qa.a: Her mother stopped telling her to try harder to stop, they saw a doctor who explained options, and now she just brings tea.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have understood Sunday before reading this letter?
qa.a: Pallavi might have thought Minakshi was upset with her, not just exhausted.

grounding: It shows a teenager who suppresses tics at school and releases them at home, tired and self-conscious, coping better when not blamed, with a doctor explaining options.

passage: "Want to know what my bus ride is like, Elizabeth? Forty minutes of holding my breath, basically. I'm Lokesh, a sixteen-year-old boy, and I've got tics. Head flicks, mostly, and a sort of cough-bark. On the bus I press my forehead against the window and try to freeze. If I let one out, the whole back row turns round. So I hold them. My neck aches by the time I get to school, and then there's six hours of the same. Then I get home and shut my door, and it's like a dam breaking. Twenty flicks in a row. I'm wiped out. My parents never tell me to stop. Dad knocks and asks, 'Dinner in ten or twenty?' That's all. Honestly, that's what helps most. At home I don't have to be on guard."

qa.q: What does Lokesh press against the bus window?
qa.a: His forehead.

qa.q: How does Lokesh feel after holding in his tics all day?
qa.a: He feels wiped out and his neck aches.

qa.q: What does Lokesh say helps most at home?
qa.a: His parents never tell him to stop; his dad just asks about dinner, so he doesn't have to be on guard.

qa.q: How might the back row on the bus see the tics if they weren't turning round?
qa.a: They might just see an ordinary passenger, and Lokesh might not feel he has to freeze for forty minutes.

grounding: It shows a teenager who suppresses tics in public and releases them at home, tired and self-conscious, who copes better when not blamed or told to stop.

passage: "Harish, you think your Bua doesn't know why you go straight to your room after school? When I was sixteen, I held my tics in all day at school. Shoulder shrugs, a little cough. I'd squeeze my fists under the desk till my nails left marks. Then I'd get home and it would all come out at once, like a pressure cooker, and I'd be so tired I'd fall asleep in my uniform. My father used to shout, 'Tanuja, stop that jerking!' It only got worse. One day my mother said, 'In this house you don't hold anything in.' And she took me to a doctor, who explained what tics are and what options there were. Nobody blamed me after that. So, in this house too, beta, you don't hold anything in."

qa.q: What did Tanuja do under her desk to hold in her tics?
qa.a: She squeezed her fists under the desk till her nails left marks.

qa.q: How did young Tanuja feel after coming home from school?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and self-conscious, releasing all the held-in tics at once and falling asleep in her uniform.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Tanuja cope better?
qa.a: Her mother said she did not have to hold anything in at home and took her to a doctor who explained tics and options, so nobody blamed her.

qa.q: How did Tanuja's mother see her daughter's tics?
qa.a: She saw them as nothing to blame Tanuja for, making home a place where Tanuja did not have to hold anything in, and sought a doctor's explanation.

grounding: An elder recalls suppressing tics at school and releasing them at home, tired and self-conscious, and coping better once not blamed and helped by a doctor's explanation.

passage: The board exam hall was dead silent, and the invigilator kept pacing. Vijay, fifteen, felt the urge to jerk his neck building like a spring. For three hours he pressed his chin down and held it, sweat on his back, one eye on the clock and the other on the long answer he still had to finish. He barely finished. At home he went up to the terrace and let the tics come: neck, shoulder, a sharp sound, over and over. His brother Tarun came up with two glasses of nimbu pani, sat on the parapet and talked about the match. He didn't say "stop." That night their mother said the doctor could see Vijay next week, to explain options since his neck was aching.

qa.q: How long did Vijay hold in his tics in the exam hall?
qa.a: He held them in for three hours.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel during and after the exam?
qa.a: He felt tense and self-conscious during it, and drained afterwards, releasing all the tics on the terrace.

qa.q: What helped Vijay cope after the exam?
qa.a: Tarun kept him company without telling him to stop, and their mother arranged for a doctor to explain options because his neck ached.

qa.q: What is it like for Tarun to sit with Vijay on the terrace?
qa.a: Tarun seems relaxed and caring; he chooses to chat about the match so Vijay does not feel watched.

grounding: Shows a teenager suppressing tics in public and releasing them at home, tired and self-conscious, coping better when not blamed, with a doctor to explain options.

passage: At his cousin's wedding in Ahmedabad, Jagdish, fourteen, stood in every family photograph with his hands clasped tight, holding back the shoulder jerk and the throat click. Aunties kept calling, "One more, beta, smile!" By the ninth photo his arms were trembling. In the car home the tics burst out one after another, and he stared out of the window, embarrassed. His older sister Ritu didn't say a word about it. She just passed him a water bottle and put on his favourite song. At home he fell asleep on the sofa. The next day Ritu said, "Your shoulder must hurt. Want to ask the doctor at your check-up about options? No pressure." Jagdish nodded.

qa.q: What did Jagdish hold back during the photographs?
qa.a: He held back the shoulder jerk and the throat click.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel in the car on the way home?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and worn out, staring out of the window as the held-back tics burst out.

qa.q: What did Ritu do right?
qa.a: She did not comment or ask him to stop, gave him water and music, and later gently offered the idea of asking a doctor about options.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel watching Jagdish struggle through the photos?
qa.a: She may feel protective and sympathetic, seeing how hard he worked to hold everything in.

grounding: Shows a teenager suppressing tics in public and releasing them later, tired and embarrassed, and a sibling who does not blame him and mentions a doctor can explain options.

passage:
Gautam dropped his school bag and, the moment the door shut, his shoulders shrugged hard three times and he let out a string of throat-clears.
"Long day?" Imran Chacha asked from the kitchen.
"I held them in for six hours. My neck hurts."
"Held them in?"
"In class, I squeeze everything tight so no one sees. Then at home they all come out at once." Gautam slumped on the sofa. "It's exhausting. And embarrassing."
"You don't have to hold anything in here. I'm not going to tell you to stop."
"Ammi sometimes does."
"I'll talk to her. And if they're causing you pain or trouble, we can see a doctor together. They can explain options. Only if you want."
Gautam shrugged again, then laughed tiredly. "Maybe. Can I just lie here first?"
"Lie there as long as you like."

qa.q: How long did Gautam say he held his tics in?
qa.a: Six hours.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel after school?
qa.a: He feels exhausted and embarrassed, with a sore neck from holding the tics in all day.

qa.q: What did Imran Chacha do well in this conversation?
qa.a: He didn't blame Gautam or tell him to stop, made home a place to release the tics, and offered a doctor visit only if Gautam wanted.

qa.q: How might Ammi's reaction change after Imran Chacha talks to her?
qa.a: She may stop telling Gautam to stop and understand that home is where he can rest from holding them in.

grounding: Gautam suppresses tics at school and releases them at home, tired and self-conscious, and copes better when not blamed, with a doctor as an option.
